questions.q: Which of the following ground-state electronic configurations represents the element with the highest first ionization enthalpy?
questions.question: Which of the following ground-state electronic configurations represents the element with the highest first ionization enthalpy?
questions.solution:
The first ionization enthalpy generally increases across a period from left to right and decreases down a group.

The given configurations correspond to:
[He] $2s^2 2p^2$: Carbon (Period 2, Group 14)
[Ne] $3s^2 3p^2$: Silicon (Period 3, Group 14)
[Ne] $3s^2 3p^3$: Phosphorus (Period 3, Group 15)
[He] $2s^2 2p^3$: Nitrogen (Period 2, Group 15)

Elements in Period 2 have higher ionization enthalpies than those in Period 3 due to their smaller atomic size. Between Carbon and Nitrogen, Nitrogen has a higher effective nuclear charge and a stable, exactly half-filled $2p$ subshell ($2p^3$). Therefore, the element with the configuration [He] $2s^2 2p^3$ has the highest first ionization enthalpy among the given options.

Answer: [He] $2s^2 2p^3$

questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Choose the INCORRECT statement regarding the elements of Group 14 and their compounds.
questions.question: Choose the INCORRECT statement regarding the elements of Group 14 and their compounds.
options: The tendency to show catenation decreases down the group.
The stability of $+2$ oxidation state increases in the sequence $\mathrm{Ge} < \mathrm{Sn} < \mathrm{Pb}$.
$\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ is a gas while $\mathrm{SiO}_{2}$ is a solid network at room temperature.
questions.solution:
Statement 1 is incorrect because carbon does not have vacant d-orbitals in its valence shell. Therefore, it cannot accept a lone pair of electrons from water molecules, making $\mathrm{CCl}_{4}$ resistant to hydrolysis. In contrast, $\mathrm{SiCl}_{4}$ undergoes hydrolysis easily.

Statement 2 is correct. Catenation tendency depends on bond strength, and the $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}$ bond is much stronger than $\mathrm{Si}-\mathrm{Si}$, $\mathrm{Ge}-\mathrm{Ge}$, etc. The tendency decreases down the group.

Statement 3 is correct due to the inert pair effect, which makes the lower oxidation state more stable for heavier elements.

Statement 4 is correct. $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ forms discrete molecules with $p\pi-p\pi$ double bonds, making it a gas. $\mathrm{SiO}_{2}$ forms a three-dimensional network solid with single bonds because silicon does not effectively form $p\pi-p\pi$ bonds.

Answer: $\mathrm{CCl}_{4}$ undergoes hydrolysis easily in water.

questions.q: Among the elements with the following atomic numbers, which one will have the highest second ionisation enthalpy?
questions.question: Among the elements with the following atomic numbers, which one will have the highest second ionisation enthalpy?
questions.solution:
The atomic numbers correspond to the following elements:
$11 \rightarrow \text{Na}$
$12 \rightarrow \text{Mg}$
$13 \rightarrow \text{Al}$
$14 \rightarrow \text{Si}$

The second ionisation enthalpy is the energy required to remove an electron from the unipositive cation ($M^+$). Let us write the electronic configurations of their $+1$ ions:
$\text{Na}^+ : 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$ (stable noble gas core)
$\text{Mg}^+ : 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1$
$\text{Al}^+ : 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2$
$\text{Si}^+ : 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^1$

Removing a second electron from $\text{Na}$ requires breaking a highly stable, fully-filled principal quantum shell (the neon core), which requires an exceptionally large amount of energy. The other ions still have valence electrons in the $n=3$ shell. Therefore, $\text{Na}$ ($Z=11$) has the highest second ionisation enthalpy.

Answer: $11$

questions.q: The first ionization enthalpies of $\text{C}$, $\text{N}$ and $\text{F}$ are $1086$, $1402$ and $1681\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ respectively. The first ionization enthalpy ($\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) of $\text{O}$ is most likely to be:
questions.question: The first ionization enthalpies of $\text{C}$, $\text{N}$ and $\text{F}$ are $1086$, $1402$ and $1681\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ respectively. The first ionization enthalpy ($\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) of $\text{O}$ is most likely to be:
questions.solution:
In the second period, the general trend is an increase in first ionization enthalpy from left to right. However, Nitrogen ($\text{Group } 15$) has a stable half-filled $2\text{p}^3$ electronic configuration, making its first ionization enthalpy higher than that of Oxygen ($\text{Group } 16$).

The correct order of first ionization enthalpies is $\text{C} < \text{O} < \text{N} < \text{F}$.

Therefore, the first ionization enthalpy of $\text{O}$ must lie strictly between that of $\text{C}$ ($1086\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) and $\text{N}$ ($1402\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$). Among the given options, only $1314\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ falls in this range.

Answer: $1314$

The first ionization enthalpies ($\Delta_{i}H$) and electron gain enthalpies ($\Delta_{eg}H$) of four elements W, X, Y and Z are given below:

Element$\Delta_{i}H$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$)$\Delta_{eg}H$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$)
W1681$-328$
X1256$-349$
Y520$-60$
Z496$-53$


If these elements correspond to $\mathrm{Li}$, $\mathrm{Na}$, $\mathrm{F}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}$ (not necessarily in that order), identify the correct assignment.
questions.question:
The first ionization enthalpies ($\Delta_{i}H$) and electron gain enthalpies ($\Delta_{eg}H$) of four elements W, X, Y and Z are given below:

Element$\Delta_{i}H$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$)$\Delta_{eg}H$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$)
W1681$-328$
X1256$-349$
Y520$-60$
Z496$-53$


If these elements correspond to $\mathrm{Li}$, $\mathrm{Na}$, $\mathrm{F}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}$ (not necessarily in that order), identify the correct assignment.
questions.solution:
Elements with high ionization enthalpy and highly negative electron gain enthalpy belong to halogens (W and X). Elements with low ionization enthalpy and slightly negative electron gain enthalpy belong to alkali metals (Y and Z).

Among halogens, $\mathrm{F}$ has a higher ionization enthalpy than $\mathrm{Cl}$, but $\mathrm{Cl}$ has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than $\mathrm{F}$ due to interelectronic repulsions in the small $2p$ subshell of $\mathrm{F}$. Thus, W is $\mathrm{F}$ and X is $\mathrm{Cl}$.

Among alkali metals, ionization enthalpy decreases down the group. Thus, $\mathrm{Li}$ has a higher ionization enthalpy than $\mathrm{Na}$. Therefore, Y is $\mathrm{Li}$ and Z is $\mathrm{Na}$.

Hence, W = $\mathrm{F}$, X = $\mathrm{Cl}$, Y = $\mathrm{Li}$, Z = $\mathrm{Na}$.

Answer: W = $\mathrm{F}$, X = $\mathrm{Cl}$, Y = $\mathrm{Li}$, Z = $\mathrm{Na}$

Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The third ionization enthalpy of Magnesium is greater than the corresponding third ionization enthalpy of Aluminum.
Statement II: Among the isoelectronic species $\mathrm{S}^{2-}$, $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$, $\mathrm{K}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$, the ionic radius of $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ is the largest.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The third ionization enthalpy of Magnesium is greater than the corresponding third ionization enthalpy of Aluminum.
Statement II: Among the isoelectronic species $\mathrm{S}^{2-}$, $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$, $\mathrm{K}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$, the ionic radius of $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ is the largest.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
questions.solution:
Statement I: The electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Mg}$ is $[\mathrm{Ne}] \ 3\mathrm{s}^{2}$ and that of $\mathrm{Al}$ is $[\mathrm{Ne}] \ 3\mathrm{s}^{2} \ 3\mathrm{p}^{1}$.
After removing two electrons, $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ acquires a stable noble gas configuration $[\mathrm{Ne}]$, whereas $\mathrm{Al}^{2+}$ has the configuration $[\mathrm{Ne}] \ 3\mathrm{s}^{1}$.
Removing a third electron from the stable noble gas core of $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ requires significantly more energy than removing the $3\mathrm{s}^{1}$ electron from $\mathrm{Al}^{2+}$. Thus, the third ionization enthalpy of $\mathrm{Mg}$ is greater than that of $\mathrm{Al}$. Statement I is true.

Statement II: The species $\mathrm{S}^{2-}$, $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$, $\mathrm{K}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ are isoelectronic, each containing $18$ electrons.
For isoelectronic species, the ionic radius decreases as the nuclear charge (number of protons) increases.
The nuclear charges are $\mathrm{S} \ (16)$, $\mathrm{Cl} \ (17)$, $\mathrm{K} \ (19)$ and $\mathrm{Ca} \ (20)$.
Since $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ has the highest nuclear charge, it exerts the strongest effective nuclear pull on the electrons, making it the smallest ion among them, not the largest. Statement II is false.

Answer: Statement I is true but Statement II is false

questions.q: A graph of $\log(\mathrm{IE}_n)$ versus the number of electrons removed ($n$) is plotted for an unknown element belonging to period 3 of the periodic table. The graph shows a moderate positive slope from $n=1$ to $n=2$, a sudden sharp vertical spike between $n=2$ and $n=3$, and a moderate slope thereafter. Based on this observation, identify the element.
questions.question: A graph of $\log(\mathrm{IE}_n)$ versus the number of electrons removed ($n$) is plotted for an unknown element belonging to period 3 of the periodic table. The graph shows a moderate positive slope from $n=1$ to $n=2$, a sudden sharp vertical spike between $n=2$ and $n=3$, and a moderate slope thereafter. Based on this observation, identify the element.
questions.solution:
The sudden sharp vertical spike in the $\log(\mathrm{IE}_n)$ versus $n$ graph between $n=2$ and $n=3$ indicates that a very large amount of energy is required to remove the third electron.

This implies that the third electron is being removed from a stable, fully-filled noble gas core. Therefore, the element has exactly 2 valence electrons.

An element with 2 valence electrons belongs to Group 2 of the periodic table.

The Group 2 element present in period 3 is Magnesium (Mg).

Answer: Magnesium (Mg)

questions.q: The first ionization enthalpy of Gallium (Ga) is higher than that of Aluminum (Al). The primary reason for this observation is :
questions.question: The first ionization enthalpy of Gallium (Ga) is higher than that of Aluminum (Al). The primary reason for this observation is :
options: the poor shielding effect of inner 3d-electrons in Gallium leading to a higher effective nuclear charge.
the high shielding effect of inner 3d-electrons in Gallium leading to a lower effective nuclear charge.
the greater atomic size of Gallium compared to Aluminum.
the inert pair effect which strongly binds the valence s-electrons in Gallium.
questions.solution:
Gallium (atomic number 31) is preceded by the 3d transition series. The 10 inner 3d-electrons provide poor shielding for the outer valence electrons against the increasing nuclear charge.

As a result, the effective nuclear charge ($Z_{\text{eff}}$) experienced by the valence electrons in Gallium is higher than expected. This makes it harder to remove an electron, resulting in a higher first ionization enthalpy for Gallium compared to Aluminum.

Answer: the poor shielding effect of inner 3d-electrons in Gallium leading to a higher effective nuclear charge.

questions.q: The correct increasing order of the second ionisation enthalpies for the elements $\text{C}$, $\text{N}$, $\text{O}$ and $\text{F}$ is:
questions.question: The correct increasing order of the second ionisation enthalpies for the elements $\text{C}$, $\text{N}$, $\text{O}$ and $\text{F}$ is:
questions.solution:
The second ionisation enthalpy is the energy required to remove an electron from the unipositive ion ($\text{M}^+$).

The electronic configurations of the unipositive ions are:
$\text{C}^+: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^1$
$\text{N}^+: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$
$\text{O}^+: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$
$\text{F}^+: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$

Generally, ionisation enthalpy increases across a period from left to right. However, $\text{O}^+$ has a highly stable half-filled $2p$ subshell ($2p^3$), which requires exceptionally high energy to remove an electron. As a result, the second ionisation enthalpy of oxygen is greater than that of fluorine.

Thus, the correct increasing order of second ionisation enthalpies is $\text{C} < \text{N} < \text{F} < \text{O}$.

Answer: $\text{C} < \text{N} < \text{F} < \text{O}$

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the properties of the $3\text{d}$ transition series elements:

Statement I: The increase in first ionization enthalpy across the $3\text{d}$ series is less steep compared to the p-block elements of the same period.
Statement II: The added $3\text{d}$ electrons effectively shield the outer $4\text{s}$ electrons, leading to a decrease in effective nuclear charge across the series.
Statement III: The first ionization enthalpies of $3\text{d}$ elements are generally higher than those of Group $2$ metals of the same period due to a higher effective nuclear charge.

Choose the correct combination of statements from the options given below:
questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the properties of the $3\text{d}$ transition series elements:

Statement I: The increase in first ionization enthalpy across the $3\text{d}$ series is less steep compared to the p-block elements of the same period.
Statement II: The added $3\text{d}$ electrons effectively shield the outer $4\text{s}$ electrons, leading to a decrease in effective nuclear charge across the series.
Statement III: The first ionization enthalpies of $3\text{d}$ elements are generally higher than those of Group $2$ metals of the same period due to a higher effective nuclear charge.

Choose the correct combination of statements from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Statement I is true: in the $3\text{d}$ series, electrons are added to the inner $3\text{d}$ subshell, which partially shields the outer $4\text{s}$ electrons from the increasing nuclear charge. This makes the increase in ionization enthalpy more gradual compared to p-block elements where electrons are added to the outermost shell.

Statement II is false: d-electrons provide poor shielding, which causes the effective nuclear charge to increase across the series, not decrease.

Statement III is true: compared to Group $2$ metals, $3\text{d}$ elements have a higher nuclear charge and poor shielding by d-electrons, resulting in a higher effective nuclear charge and thus higher first ionization enthalpies.

Therefore, only statements I and III are correct.

Answer: I and III only

questions.q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Among the hydrides of group 16 elements, the one with the lowest boiling point is $\mathrm{H_2S}$.
Statement II: The central atom of the group 16 hydride with the highest boiling point can show a maximum covalency of 6.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Among the hydrides of group 16 elements, the one with the lowest boiling point is $\mathrm{H_2S}$.
Statement II: The central atom of the group 16 hydride with the highest boiling point can show a maximum covalency of 6.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
questions.solution:
The boiling point of group 16 hydrides follows the order: $\mathrm{H_2S} < \mathrm{H_2Se} < \mathrm{H_2Te} < \mathrm{H_2O}$. The anomalously high boiling point of water is due to strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Thus, $\mathrm{H_2S}$ has the lowest boiling point, making Statement I true.

The hydride with the highest boiling point is $\mathrm{H_2O}$, and its central atom is oxygen. Since oxygen belongs to the second period, it does not have vacant d-orbitals in its valence shell. Therefore, it cannot expand its octet and its maximum covalency is restricted to 4. Thus, Statement II is false.

Answer: Statement I is true but Statement II is false

questions.q: The first ionization enthalpies of four consecutive elements of the third period are $496$, $577$, $737$ and $786\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Which of the following is the first ionization enthalpy ($\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) of the element that possesses the highest second ionization enthalpy among these four?
questions.question: The first ionization enthalpies of four consecutive elements of the third period are $496$, $577$, $737$ and $786\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Which of the following is the first ionization enthalpy ($\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) of the element that possesses the highest second ionization enthalpy among these four?
questions.solution:
The given first ionization enthalpies belong to four consecutive elements of the third period: $\text{Na}$, $\text{Mg}$, $\text{Al}$, and $\text{Si}$.

The general trend is an increase in ionization enthalpy across a period, but $\text{Mg}$ ($\text{Group } 2$, $3\text{s}^2$) has a higher first ionization enthalpy than $\text{Al}$ ($\text{Group } 13$, $3\text{s}^2 3\text{p}^1$) due to the stability of the fully-filled s-subshell.

Mapping the values to the elements:
$\text{Na} = 496\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
$\text{Al} = 577\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
$\text{Mg} = 737\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
$\text{Si} = 786\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

The second ionization enthalpy involves removing an electron from the unipositive cation.
$\text{Na}^+$ has a highly stable noble gas core configuration ($1\text{s}^2 2\text{s}^2 2\text{p}^6$, isoelectronic with $\text{Ne}$). Removing an electron from this stable core requires a very large amount of energy.

Thus, $\text{Na}$ has the highest second ionization enthalpy among these elements. Its first ionization enthalpy is $496\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: $496$

questions.q:
Four hypothetical elements P, Q, R, and S belong to groups $g$ and $g+1$, and periods $p$ and $p+1$ of the p-block (excluding anomalous groups like 15/16 or 17/18).

The order of their atomic radii is P < Q < R < S.
The order of their first ionization enthalpies is S < R < Q < P.

Which of the following correctly represents their positions in the periodic table?
questions.question:
Four hypothetical elements P, Q, R, and S belong to groups $g$ and $g+1$, and periods $p$ and $p+1$ of the p-block (excluding anomalous groups like 15/16 or 17/18).

The order of their atomic radii is P < Q < R < S.
The order of their first ionization enthalpies is S < R < Q < P.

Which of the following correctly represents their positions in the periodic table?
questions.solution:
Atomic radius generally decreases across a period from left to right and increases down a group. First ionization enthalpy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.

Given the order of atomic radii is P < Q < R < S, P must be the element at the top-right (smallest) and S must be the element at the bottom-left (largest).

Between the top-left element and the bottom-right element, the increase in size down a group is more significant than the decrease across a period. Therefore, the top-left element is smaller than the bottom-right element. This means Q is at the top-left and R is at the bottom-right.

Thus, the positions are:
Period $p$: Q (Group $g$), P (Group $g+1$)
Period $p+1$: S (Group $g$), R (Group $g+1$)

Checking the ionization enthalpy for this arrangement: S (bottom-left) has the lowest IE and P (top-right) has the highest IE. The decrease in IE down a group is generally larger than the increase across a period, so R (bottom-right) < Q (top-left). The overall order is S < R < Q < P, which matches the given condition.

Answer: Period $p$: Q (Group $g$), P (Group $g+1$)
Period $p+1$: S (Group $g$), R (Group $g+1$)

questions.q: The first ionisation enthalpies of four elements $\text{Be}$, $\text{B}$, $\text{N}$ and $\text{O}$ are $801$, $899$, $1314$ and $1402 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (not necessarily in that order). The correct assignment of the first ionisation enthalpies to the respective elements is:
questions.question: The first ionisation enthalpies of four elements $\text{Be}$, $\text{B}$, $\text{N}$ and $\text{O}$ are $801$, $899$, $1314$ and $1402 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (not necessarily in that order). The correct assignment of the first ionisation enthalpies to the respective elements is:
questions.solution:
The first ionisation enthalpy generally increases across a period from left to right due to an increase in effective nuclear charge. However, there are exceptions due to the extra stability of fully-filled and half-filled subshells.

For the given elements, $\text{Be}$ ($1s^2 2s^2$) has a fully-filled $2s$ subshell, making its first ionisation enthalpy higher than that of $\text{B}$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^1$).

Similarly, $\text{N}$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$) has a stable half-filled $2p$ subshell, making its first ionisation enthalpy higher than that of $\text{O}$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$).

Therefore, the correct increasing order of first ionisation enthalpies is $\text{B} < \text{Be} < \text{O} < \text{N}$.

Arranging the given values in increasing order: $801 < 899 < 1314 < 1402 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Matching the elements with the values gives: $\text{B} = 801$, $\text{Be} = 899$, $\text{O} = 1314$, and $\text{N} = 1402 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: $\text{Be} = 899$, $\text{B} = 801$, $\text{N} = 1402$, $\text{O} = 1314$

questions.q: Elements X, Y, and Z belong to the third period of the periodic table and have atomic numbers $11$, $14$, and $17$, respectively. Which of the following correctly describes the relative chemical reactivity of these elements and the acid-base nature of the oxides formed by X and Z?
questions.question: Elements X, Y, and Z belong to the third period of the periodic table and have atomic numbers $11$, $14$, and $17$, respectively. Which of the following correctly describes the relative chemical reactivity of these elements and the acid-base nature of the oxides formed by X and Z?
options: The chemical reactivity is highest for X and Z and lowest for Y; the oxide of X is basic while that of Z is acidic.
The chemical reactivity steadily increases from X to Z; the oxide of X is basic while that of Z is acidic.
The chemical reactivity steadily decreases from X to Z; the oxide of X is acidic while that of Z is basic.
The chemical reactivity is highest for X and Z and lowest for Y; the oxide of X is acidic while that of Z is basic.
questions.solution:
The elements with atomic numbers $11$, $14$, and $17$ in the third period are Sodium (Na), Silicon (Si), and Chlorine (Cl), respectively.

Across a period, chemical reactivity is highest at the two extremes (excluding noble gases) and lowest in the centre. Thus, X (Group 1) and Z (Group 17) are highly reactive, while Y (Group 14) is less reactive.

The nature of oxides changes from strongly basic on the left to strongly acidic on the right. Therefore, the oxide of X (Na) is basic, and the oxide of Z (Cl) is acidic.

Answer: The chemical reactivity is highest for X and Z and lowest for Y; the oxide of X is basic while that of Z is acidic.

questions.q:
Consider the elements $\text{Na}$, $\text{Al}$, $\text{P}$, and $\text{Cl}$ from the third period of the periodic table. Identify the correct statements from the following:
(A) The first ionization enthalpy of $\text{P}$ is lower than that of $\text{Na}$.
(B) The oxide of $\text{Na}$ is basic while the oxide of $\text{Cl}$ is strongly acidic.
(C) $\text{Na}$ and $\text{Cl}$ combine to form a primarily covalent compound.
(D) $\text{Al}$ forms an amphoteric oxide.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
Consider the elements $\text{Na}$, $\text{Al}$, $\text{P}$, and $\text{Cl}$ from the third period of the periodic table. Identify the correct statements from the following:
(A) The first ionization enthalpy of $\text{P}$ is lower than that of $\text{Na}$.
(B) The oxide of $\text{Na}$ is basic while the oxide of $\text{Cl}$ is strongly acidic.
(C) $\text{Na}$ and $\text{Cl}$ combine to form a primarily covalent compound.
(D) $\text{Al}$ forms an amphoteric oxide.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Across a period, non-metallic character increases, which generally corresponds to an increase in first ionization enthalpy. Thus, $\text{P}$ (a non-metal) has a higher first ionization enthalpy than $\text{Na}$ (a metal), making statement (A) incorrect.

Oxides of highly reactive metals like $\text{Na}$ are basic (e.g., $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$), while oxides of non-metals like $\text{Cl}$ are acidic (e.g., $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$). Thus, statement (B) is correct.

$\text{Na}$ is a highly electropositive metal and $\text{Cl}$ is a highly electronegative non-metal. The large electronegativity difference between them leads to the formation of an ionic bond, making statement (C) incorrect.

Aluminium forms $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, which is a well-known amphoteric oxide. Thus, statement (D) is correct.

Therefore, the correct statements are (B) and (D) only.

Answer: (B) and (D) only

questions.q:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The first electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is negative, while its second electron gain enthalpy is positive.
Statement II: The first electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is less negative than that of sulphur due to high interelectronic repulsion in its compact 2p subshell.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
questions.question:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The first electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is negative, while its second electron gain enthalpy is positive.
Statement II: The first electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is less negative than that of sulphur due to high interelectronic repulsion in its compact 2p subshell.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
questions.solution:
Statement I is true. The addition of the first electron to a neutral oxygen atom is an exothermic process, resulting in a negative first electron gain enthalpy. However, adding a second electron to the negatively charged $O^{-}$ ion is strongly opposed by electrostatic repulsion. Energy must be supplied to overcome this repulsion, making the second electron gain enthalpy positive.

Statement II is true. Oxygen has a smaller atomic size compared to sulphur. The added electron in oxygen goes into the compact 2p subshell, which experiences significant interelectronic repulsion. In sulphur, the added electron enters the larger 3p subshell, where repulsion is much less. Consequently, the first electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is less negative than that of sulphur.

Therefore, both Statement I and Statement II are true.

Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true

questions.q: First ionisation enthalpy values of four consecutive period 2 elements (C, N, O, F) are given below. Choose the correct value for the element whose homonuclear diatomic molecule is paramagnetic in nature :
questions.question: First ionisation enthalpy values of four consecutive period 2 elements (C, N, O, F) are given below. Choose the correct value for the element whose homonuclear diatomic molecule is paramagnetic in nature :
questions.solution:
The four consecutive period 2 elements given are C, N, O, and F.

According to Molecular Orbital Theory, among their homonuclear diatomic molecules ($\mathrm{C}_2$, $\mathrm{N}_2$, $\mathrm{O}_2$, $\mathrm{F}_2$), only $\mathrm{O}_2$ contains unpaired electrons in its anti-bonding $\pi^{*}$ molecular orbitals, making it paramagnetic.

questions.question:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The first ionization enthalpy of Nitrogen is greater than that of Oxygen.
Statement II: The second ionization enthalpy of Nitrogen is greater than that of Oxygen.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
questions.solution:
The electronic configuration of neutral Nitrogen (N) is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$ and that of Oxygen (O) is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$.

Nitrogen has an exactly half-filled $2p$ subshell, which provides extra stability. Therefore, it requires more energy to remove the first electron from Nitrogen than from Oxygen. Thus, Statement I is true.

The second ionization enthalpy involves removing an electron from the unipositive cations.
The electronic configuration of N$^+$ is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$.
The electronic configuration of O$^+$ is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$.

Now, the O$^+$ ion has the stable exactly half-filled $2p$ subshell. Consequently, removing an electron from O$^+$ requires more energy than removing one from N$^+$. The second ionization enthalpy of Oxygen is greater than that of Nitrogen. Thus, Statement II is false.

Answer: Statement I is true but Statement II is false

questions.question: Consider four elements P, Q, R, and S belonging to the third period of the periodic table. P has the lowest first ionization enthalpy in the period, Q has the most negative electron gain enthalpy, R forms an amphoteric oxide, and S has a positive electron gain enthalpy. Identify the INCORRECT statement regarding the properties of these elements.
options: P and Q are highly reactive, while S is the least reactive element among them.
The chemical reactivity steadily increases from P to Q across the period.
The oxide formed by P is basic in nature, whereas the oxides formed by Q are acidic.
The high reactivity of P is due to its low ionization enthalpy, while that of Q is due to its highly negative electron gain enthalpy.
questions.solution:
Based on the given properties for the third period elements:
P has the lowest first ionization enthalpy, so it is Sodium (Na, Group 1).
Q has the most negative electron gain enthalpy, so it is Chlorine (Cl, Group 17).
R forms an amphoteric oxide, so it is Aluminium (Al, Group 13).
S has a positive electron gain enthalpy, so it is Argon (Ar, Group 18).

Chemical reactivity across a period is highest at the extremes (Group 1 and Group 17) due to the ease of losing and gaining electrons, respectively. It is lowest in the middle. Therefore, reactivity does not steadily increase from P to Q; it follows a U-shaped trend. This makes the statement claiming a steady increase incorrect.

P (Na) forms basic oxides and Q (Cl) forms acidic oxides. S (Ar) is a noble gas and is the least reactive.

Answer: The chemical reactivity steadily increases from P to Q across the period.

questions.question:
If the first ionisation enthalpy of the elements of the third period (from $Z = 11$ to $Z = 18$) is plotted against their atomic numbers, the graph generally shows an upward trend. However, there are specific 'dips' where the ionisation enthalpy of an element is lower than that of the immediately preceding element.

Identify the pair of atomic numbers corresponding to the elements where these dips occur.
questions.solution:
Across the third period (from $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Ar}$), the first ionisation enthalpy generally increases due to an increase in effective nuclear charge.

However, exceptions occur due to the extra stability of fully-filled and half-filled subshells:
1. $\text{Mg}$ ($Z = 12$) has a stable $3s^2$ configuration, whereas $\text{Al}$ ($Z = 13$) has a $3s^2 3p^1$ configuration. It is easier to remove the $3p^1$ electron of $\text{Al}$ than a $3s$ electron of $\text{Mg}$. Thus, a dip occurs at $Z = 13$.
2. $\text{P}$ ($Z = 15$) has a stable half-filled $3s^2 3p^3$ configuration, whereas $\text{S}$ ($Z = 16$) has a $3s^2 3p^4$ configuration. It is easier to remove the paired $3p$ electron of $\text{S}$ than an unpaired electron from $\text{P}$. Thus, another dip occurs at $Z = 16$.

Therefore, the dips occur at atomic numbers $13$ and $16$.

Answer: $13$ and $16$

questions.question: The correct decreasing order of the second ionization enthalpies ($IE_2$) for the elements C, N, O, and F is
questions.solution:
The second ionization enthalpy ($IE_2$) is the energy required to remove an electron from the monovalent cation ($\text{M}^+$) of an element.

The electronic configurations of the unipositive cations are:
$\text{C}^+$: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^1$
$\text{N}^+$: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$
$\text{O}^+$: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$
$\text{F}^+$: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$

Generally, ionization enthalpy increases from left to right across a period due to an increase in effective nuclear charge. This gives the expected order $\text{C}^+ < \text{N}^+ < \text{O}^+ < \text{F}^+$.

However, the $\text{O}^+$ cation has a stable, exactly half-filled $2p^3$ configuration. Removing an electron from this stable configuration requires exceptionally high energy, making the second ionization enthalpy of Oxygen greater than that of Fluorine.

Thus, the correct decreasing order of second ionization enthalpies is $\text{O} > \text{F} > \text{N} > \text{C}$.

Answer: $\text{O} > \text{F} > \text{N} > \text{C}$

Because of this extra stability, removing an electron from $\mathrm{O}^{+}$ requires more energy than removing one from $\mathrm{F}^{+}$ ($2\mathrm{p}^{4}$).

Therefore, the second ionization enthalpy of Oxygen is exceptionally high, making it greater than that of Fluorine.

The correct increasing order of second ionization enthalpies is $\mathrm{C} < \mathrm{N} < \mathrm{F} < \mathrm{O}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{C} < \mathrm{N} < \mathrm{F} < \mathrm{O}$

II. The order of atomic radius is B < A < D < C.

questions.question:
Consider four elements A, B, C, and D placed in a $2 \times 2$ grid in the p-block of the periodic table. Element A is in Group 15, Period 2; B is in Group 16, Period 2; C is in Group 15, Period 3; and D is in Group 16, Period 3.

Evaluate the following statements regarding their properties:
I. The order of first ionization enthalpy is D < C < B < A.
II. The order of atomic radius is B < A < D < C.
III. The order of negative electron gain enthalpy is C < A < B < D.
IV. The order of electronegativity is C < D < A < B.

Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
The elements are A (Nitrogen, N), B (Oxygen, O), C (Phosphorus, P), and D (Sulphur, S).

Statement I: First ionization enthalpy generally increases across a period, but Group 15 elements have higher IE than Group 16 due to half-filled stable electronic configuration. Thus, N > O and P > S. Down the group, IE decreases, so N > P and O > S. The overall order is S < P < O < N, which corresponds to D < C < B < A. Statement I is correct.

Statement II: Atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group. Thus, O < N and S < P. Also, Period 2 elements are smaller than Period 3 elements. The overall order is O < N < S < P, which corresponds to B < A < D < C. Statement II is correct.

Statement III: Nitrogen has a positive electron gain enthalpy, making its negative electron gain enthalpy the lowest. Between O and S, S has a more negative electron gain enthalpy due to less inter-electronic repulsion in the 3p subshell compared to the compact 2p subshell of O. The order of negative electron gain enthalpy is N < P < O < S, which corresponds to A < C < B < D. Statement III is incorrect.

Statement IV: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group. The order is P < S < N < O, which corresponds to C < D < A < B. Statement IV is correct.

Therefore, statements I, II, and IV are correct.

Answer: I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Second ionization enthalpy ($\mathrm{IE}_2$) is the energy required to remove an electron from the univalent gaseous cation ($M^+$).

The valence electronic configurations of the univalent cations are:
$\mathrm{C}^+ : 2s^2 2p^1$
$\mathrm{N}^+ : 2s^2 2p^2$
$\mathrm{O}^+ : 2s^2 2p^3$
$\mathrm{F}^+ : 2s^2 2p^4$

The $\mathrm{O}^+$ ion has an exactly half-filled $2p^3$ subshell, which imparts extra stability. Removing an electron from this stable configuration requires exceptionally high energy, making the $\mathrm{IE}_2$ of oxygen the highest among these four elements.

For the remaining ions ($\mathrm{C}^+, \mathrm{N}^+, \mathrm{F}^+$), the effective nuclear charge increases from carbon to fluorine, so the energy required to remove the next electron follows the general trend: $\mathrm{C} < \mathrm{N} < \mathrm{F}$.

Thus, the correct increasing order of second ionization enthalpy is $\mathrm{C} < \mathrm{N} < \mathrm{F} < \mathrm{O}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{C} < \mathrm{N} < \mathrm{F} < \mathrm{O}$

questions.question:
The first, second and third ionization enthalpies (in $\mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$) for two elements $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ belonging to Period 3 are given below:

Element$\mathrm{IE_1}$$\mathrm{IE_2}$$\mathrm{IE_3}$
$\mathrm{X}$$496$$4562$$6910$
$\mathrm{Y}$$737$$1451$$7733$


Based on the given data, identify the most stable ions formed by $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ that are isoelectronic with Neon, and the correct relationship between their ionic radii.
options: Stable ions are $\mathrm{X}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Y}^{2+}$, and ionic radius of $\mathrm{X}^{+} > \mathrm{Y}^{2+}$
Stable ions are $\mathrm{X}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Y}^{2+}$, and ionic radius of $\mathrm{X}^{+} < \mathrm{Y}^{2+}$
Stable ions are $\mathrm{X}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Y}^{+}$, and ionic radius of $\mathrm{X}^{2+} > \mathrm{Y}^{+}$
Stable ions are $\mathrm{X}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Y}^{+}$, and ionic radius of $\mathrm{X}^{2+} < \mathrm{Y}^{+}$
questions.solution:
From the given data, element $\mathrm{X}$ shows a massive jump between $\mathrm{IE_1}$ and $\mathrm{IE_2}$ ($496$ to $4562 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$). This indicates that removing the second electron disrupts a stable noble gas core, meaning $\mathrm{X}$ has $1$ valence electron. Thus, its most stable ion is $\mathrm{X}^{+}$.

Element $\mathrm{Y}$ shows a massive jump between $\mathrm{IE_2}$ and $\mathrm{IE_3}$ ($1451$ to $7733 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$), indicating it has $2$ valence electrons. Its most stable ion is $\mathrm{Y}^{2+}$.

Since both elements belong to Period 3, $\mathrm{X}$ is Sodium ($\mathrm{Na}$) and $\mathrm{Y}$ is Magnesium ($\mathrm{Mg}$). Their stable ions $\mathrm{X}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Y}^{2+}$ are isoelectronic with Neon ($10$ electrons).

For isoelectronic species, the ionic radius is inversely proportional to the nuclear charge. Element $\mathrm{Y}$ ($\mathrm{Mg}$, $Z=12$) has a higher nuclear charge than element $\mathrm{X}$ ($\mathrm{Na}$, $Z=11$). Therefore, the nucleus of $\mathrm{Y}^{2+}$ attracts the $10$ electrons more strongly than $\mathrm{X}^{+}$, making the ionic radius of $\mathrm{X}^{+}$ greater than that of $\mathrm{Y}^{2+}$.

Answer: Stable ions are $\mathrm{X}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Y}^{2+}$, and ionic radius of $\mathrm{X}^{+} > \mathrm{Y}^{2+}$

Elements X and Y have electron gain enthalpies of $-348 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $-295 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ respectively.

Assuming X and Y are monovalent non-metals, what are the correct formulas for the compounds formed by M with X and Y, and the correct order of their ionic character?
questions.question:
The first, second and third ionisation enthalpies of a metal M are $590 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $1145 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $4912 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ respectively.

Elements X and Y have electron gain enthalpies of $-348 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $-295 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ respectively.

Assuming X and Y are monovalent non-metals, what are the correct formulas for the compounds formed by M with X and Y, and the correct order of their ionic character?
questions.solution:
The successive ionisation enthalpies of metal M show a sudden, large jump between the second ($1145 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) and third ($4912 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) ionisation enthalpies.

This indicates that M has two valence electrons and will form an $\text{M}^{2+}$ ion.

Since X and Y are monovalent non-metals (forming $\text{X}^{-}$ and $\text{Y}^{-}$ ions), the formulas of the compounds formed will be $\text{MX}_2$ and $\text{MY}_2$.

The ionic character of a bond increases with the tendency of the non-metal to accept an electron, which corresponds to a more negative electron gain enthalpy.

Since the magnitude of the negative electron gain enthalpy of X ($|-348| \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) is greater than that of Y ($|-295| \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$), X has a higher tendency to form an anion.

Therefore, the compound $\text{MX}_2$ will have a higher ionic character than $\text{MY}_2$, giving the correct order as $\text{MX}_2 > \text{MY}_2$.

Answer: $\text{MX}_2 \text{ and MY}_2 ; \text{MX}_2 > \text{MY}_2$

questions.question: Identify the correct increasing order of the magnitude of negative electron gain enthalpy for the following elements: O, S, F, and Cl.
questions.solution:
Halogens (Group 17) have a higher effective nuclear charge than chalcogens (Group 16) in the same period, resulting in a more negative electron gain enthalpy. Thus, F and Cl have higher magnitudes than O and S.

Within Group 17, Cl has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than F. The small size of the F atom leads to high interelectronic repulsion in its compact 2p subshell, making the addition of an electron less favorable than in the larger 3p subshell of Cl.

Similarly, within Group 16, S has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than O due to the same size and repulsion factors.

Comparing the magnitudes, the correct increasing order is O < S < F < Cl.

Answer: O < S < F < Cl

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the elements of Group 13:
(A) The atomic radius of $\text{Ga}$ is smaller than that of $\text{Al}$.
(B) The first ionization enthalpy of $\text{Tl}$ is greater than that of $\text{Ga}$.
(C) Electronegativity continuously decreases down the group from $\text{B}$ to $\text{Tl}$.
(D) The increase in effective nuclear charge from $\text{Al}$ to $\text{Ga}$ is significantly higher than that from $\text{B}$ to $\text{Al}$ due to the poor shielding of 3d electrons.

Choose the correct statements from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Statement (A) is correct. The atomic radius of $\text{Ga}$ (135 pm) is less than that of $\text{Al}$ (143 pm) due to the poor shielding effect of the ten 3d electrons in $\text{Ga}$.

Statement (B) is correct. The first ionization enthalpy of $\text{Tl}$ (589 kJ/mol) is greater than that of $\text{Ga}$ (579 kJ/mol). This is due to the poor shielding effect of both 4f and 5d electrons in $\text{Tl}$, which significantly increases the effective nuclear charge on its valence electrons.

Statement (C) is incorrect. The electronegativity of Group 13 elements first decreases from $\text{B}$ (2.0) to $\text{Al}$ (1.5) and then marginally increases down the group to $\text{Ga}$ (1.6), $\text{In}$ (1.7) and $\text{Tl}$ (1.8) due to the discrepancies in atomic size and effective nuclear charge.

Statement (D) is correct. The presence of completely filled d-orbitals in $\text{Ga}$ provides poor shielding, leading to a much higher increase in effective nuclear charge from $\text{Al}$ to $\text{Ga}$ compared to the transition from $\text{B}$ to $\text{Al}$.

Therefore, statements (A), (B) and (D) are correct.

Answer: (A), (B) and (D) only

O$^+$ : $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$
F$^+$ : $1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$

Generally, ionization enthalpy increases across a period from left to right due to an increase in effective nuclear charge. Based on this general trend, the expected order would be C$^+$ < N$^+$ < O$^+$ < F$^+$.

However, O$^+$ has an exactly half-filled $2p$ subshell ($2p^3$), which imparts extra stability. Removing an electron from this stable configuration requires more energy than removing an electron from F$^+$ (which has a $2p^4$ configuration and relieves inter-electronic repulsion upon losing an electron to become half-filled).

Therefore, the second ionization enthalpy of Oxygen is exceptionally high and exceeds that of Fluorine. The correct increasing order is C < N < F < O.

Answer: C < N < F < O

A plot of first ionization enthalpy versus atomic number for the elements of the second period ($\text{Li}$ to $\text{Ne}$) shows points sequentially labeled A through H. The graph exhibits a general upward trend but features two distinct dips: the ionization enthalpy of C is lower than that of B, and the ionization enthalpy of F is lower than that of E.

Identify the incorrect statement regarding this trend.
questions.question:
A plot of first ionization enthalpy versus atomic number for the elements of the second period ($\text{Li}$ to $\text{Ne}$) shows points sequentially labeled A through H. The graph exhibits a general upward trend but features two distinct dips: the ionization enthalpy of C is lower than that of B, and the ionization enthalpy of F is lower than that of E.

Identify the incorrect statement regarding this trend.
options: The element A has the lowest first ionization enthalpy in the period because its valence electron experiences the lowest effective nuclear charge.
The decrease in ionization enthalpy from B to C occurs because the $2p$ electron in C is easier to remove than the fully filled $2s$ electron in B.
The element H has the highest first ionization enthalpy in the period due to its highly stable $ns^2np^6$ electronic configuration.
The higher ionization enthalpy of E compared to F is primarily due to the completely filled $2s$ subshell in E.
questions.solution:
The elements of the second period sequentially from A to H are $\text{Li}$, $\text{Be}$, $\text{B}$, $\text{C}$, $\text{N}$, $\text{O}$, $\text{F}$, and $\text{Ne}$.

Element A ($\text{Li}$) has the lowest effective nuclear charge in the period, resulting in the lowest first ionization enthalpy.

Element B is $\text{Be}$ ($1s^2 2s^2$) and element C is $\text{B}$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^1$). The dip from B to C is due to the removal of a $2p$ electron in Boron, which is at a higher energy level and easier to remove than the $2s$ electron in Beryllium.

Element H ($\text{Ne}$) has a stable octet configuration ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$), giving it the highest ionization enthalpy in the period.

Element E is $\text{N}$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$) and element F is $\text{O}$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$). The higher ionization enthalpy of Nitrogen compared to Oxygen is due to the extra stability of its exactly half-filled $2p$ subshell, not its completely filled $2s$ subshell (which Oxygen also possesses). Therefore, the statement attributing the higher ionization enthalpy of E to a completely filled $2s$ subshell is incorrect.

Answer: The higher ionization enthalpy of E compared to F is primarily due to the completely filled $2s$ subshell in E.

questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Which of the following correctly represents the relationship between the atomic radii of Aluminium ($\text{Al}$) and Gallium ($\text{Ga}$) along with the appropriate reason?
questions.question: Which of the following correctly represents the relationship between the atomic radii of Aluminium ($\text{Al}$) and Gallium ($\text{Ga}$) along with the appropriate reason?
options: $r_{\text{Ga}} < r_{\text{Al}}$ due to the poor shielding effect of completely filled 3d orbitals in $\text{Ga}$.
$r_{\text{Ga}} > r_{\text{Al}}$ due to the addition of a new principal quantum shell in $\text{Ga}$.
$r_{\text{Ga}} < r_{\text{Al}}$ due to the lanthanoid contraction experienced by $\text{Ga}$.
$r_{\text{Ga}} > r_{\text{Al}}$ due to the high screening effect of completely filled 3d orbitals in $\text{Ga}$.
questions.solution:
The atomic radius generally increases down a group due to the addition of new electron shells. However, in Group 13, Gallium ($\text{Ga}$) has the electronic configuration $[\text{Ar}] 3\text{d}^{10} 4\text{s}^{2} 4\text{p}^{1}$. The completely filled 3d electrons offer poor shielding (or screening) for the outer electrons from the increased nuclear charge. As a result, the effective nuclear charge increases, pulling the valence electrons closer to the nucleus. This causes the atomic radius of $\text{Ga}$ (135 pm) to be smaller than that of $\text{Al}$ (143 pm).

Answer: $r_{\text{Ga}} < r_{\text{Al}}$ due to the poor shielding effect of completely filled 3d orbitals in $\text{Ga}$.

questions.q: The first six successive ionisation energies of an unknown period 3 element $\mathrm{M}$ are $1012, 1900, 2910, 4960, 6270$ and $21267 \mathrm{~kJ/mol}$, respectively. Predict the formula and the chemical nature of the highest oxide of this element.
questions.question: The first six successive ionisation energies of an unknown period 3 element $\mathrm{M}$ are $1012, 1900, 2910, 4960, 6270$ and $21267 \mathrm{~kJ/mol}$, respectively. Predict the formula and the chemical nature of the highest oxide of this element.
questions.solution:
Let us analyze the successive ionisation energies to find the maximum jump:
$\mathrm{IE}_2 / \mathrm{IE}_1 = 1900 / 1012 \approx 1.88$
$\mathrm{IE}_3 / \mathrm{IE}_2 = 2910 / 1900 \approx 1.53$
$\mathrm{IE}_4 / \mathrm{IE}_3 = 4960 / 2910 \approx 1.70$
$\mathrm{IE}_5 / \mathrm{IE}_4 = 6270 / 4960 \approx 1.26$
$\mathrm{IE}_6 / \mathrm{IE}_5 = 21267 / 6270 \approx 3.39$

The largest jump occurs between the 5th and 6th ionisation energies. This indicates that the element has 5 valence electrons, as the 6th electron is removed from a stable noble gas core.

An element with 5 valence electrons belongs to Group 15. Since it is a period 3 element, it is Phosphorus ($\mathrm{P}$).

The highest oxidation state for Group 15 elements is $+5$, so the formula of its highest oxide is $\mathrm{M}_2\mathrm{O}_5$ (like $\mathrm{P}_2\mathrm{O}_5$).

Phosphorus is a non-metal, and its higher oxides are strongly acidic in nature.

Answer: $\mathrm{M}_2\mathrm{O}_5$, Acidic

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the properties of group-17 elements:

A. The magnitude of negative electron gain enthalpy of $\text{F}$ is less than that of $\text{Cl}$.
B. The bond dissociation enthalpy of $\text{F}_2$ is less than that of $\text{Cl}_2$.
C. The standard reduction potential of $\text{F}_2$ is lower than that of $\text{Cl}_2$.
D. The magnitude of hydration enthalpy of $\text{F}^{-}$ ion is greater than that of $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ion.

Choose the correct statements from the options given below:
questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the properties of group-17 elements:

A. The magnitude of negative electron gain enthalpy of $\text{F}$ is less than that of $\text{Cl}$.
B. The bond dissociation enthalpy of $\text{F}_2$ is less than that of $\text{Cl}_2$.
C. The standard reduction potential of $\text{F}_2$ is lower than that of $\text{Cl}_2$.
D. The magnitude of hydration enthalpy of $\text{F}^{-}$ ion is greater than that of $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ion.

Choose the correct statements from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Statement A is correct: Due to the small size of the $\text{F}$ atom and strong interelectronic repulsions in the $2\text{p}$ subshell, its electron gain enthalpy is less negative than that of $\text{Cl}$.

Statement B is correct: The bond dissociation enthalpy of $\text{F}_2$ is anomalously low due to strong lone pair-lone pair repulsions between the small $\text{F}$ atoms.

Statement C is incorrect: $\text{F}_2$ is a stronger oxidizing agent than $\text{Cl}_2$, meaning it has a higher standard reduction potential. This is because the low bond dissociation enthalpy of $\text{F}_2$ and the high hydration enthalpy of the $\text{F}^{-}$ ion more than compensate for its lower electron gain enthalpy.

Statement D is correct: Hydration enthalpy is inversely proportional to ionic radius. Since $\text{F}^{-}$ is smaller than $\text{Cl}^{-}$, it has a higher magnitude of hydration enthalpy.

Therefore, statements A, B, and D are correct.

Answer: A, B and D only

Given below are four statements regarding the properties of p-block elements and their hydrides:
A. The boiling point order of group 17 hydrides is $\mathrm{HCl} < \mathrm{HBr} < \mathrm{HI} < \mathrm{HF}$.
B. The halogen forming the most thermally stable hydride has the most negative electron gain enthalpy.
C. The group 15 element forming a hydride with the lowest boiling point can show a maximum covalency of 6.
D. The bond angle in group 15 hydrides ($\mathrm{EH_3}$) decreases down the group.
Choose the correct statements from the options given below:
questions.question:
Given below are four statements regarding the properties of p-block elements and their hydrides:
A. The boiling point order of group 17 hydrides is $\mathrm{HCl} < \mathrm{HBr} < \mathrm{HI} < \mathrm{HF}$.
B. The halogen forming the most thermally stable hydride has the most negative electron gain enthalpy.
C. The group 15 element forming a hydride with the lowest boiling point can show a maximum covalency of 6.
D. The bond angle in group 15 hydrides ($\mathrm{EH_3}$) decreases down the group.
Choose the correct statements from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Statement A is correct: Due to strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding, $\mathrm{HF}$ has the highest boiling point among hydrogen halides. The correct order is $\mathrm{HCl} < \mathrm{HBr} < \mathrm{HI} < \mathrm{HF}$.

Statement B is incorrect: The most thermally stable hydride is $\mathrm{HF}$ because the $\mathrm{H-F}$ bond length is the shortest and its bond dissociation enthalpy is the highest. However, fluorine has a less negative electron gain enthalpy than chlorine due to its small size and strong interelectronic repulsions.

Statement C is correct: Among group 15 hydrides, $\mathrm{PH_3}$ has the lowest boiling point (the general order is $\mathrm{PH_3} < \mathrm{AsH_3} < \mathrm{NH_3} < \mathrm{SbH_3} < \mathrm{BiH_3}$). The central atom is phosphorus, which belongs to the third period. Due to the availability of vacant d-orbitals, it can expand its octet and show a maximum covalency of 6 (e.g., in $\mathrm{PF_6^-}$).

Statement D is correct: The bond angle in group 15 hydrides decreases down the group ($\mathrm{NH_3} > \mathrm{PH_3} > \mathrm{AsH_3} > \mathrm{SbH_3}$). As the size of the central atom increases and its electronegativity decreases, the bond pair-bond pair repulsion decreases, leading to a decrease in the bond angle.

Therefore, the correct statements are A, C, and D.

Answer: A, C and D only

questions.q: An element is located in Period 7 and Group 14 of the modern periodic table. The three-letter IUPAC symbol for this element is
questions.question: An element is located in Period 7 and Group 14 of the modern periodic table. The three-letter IUPAC symbol for this element is
questions.solution:
The position of the element is given as Period 7 and Group 14.

Period 7 indicates that the outermost shell is $n = 7$.
Group 14 belongs to the p-block of the periodic table. For p-block elements, the group number is $10 + \text{number of valence electrons}$.
Thus, the element has $4$ valence electrons, corresponding to the outer configuration $7\text{s}^{2} 7\text{p}^{2}$.

To find the atomic number ($Z$), we start from the preceding noble gas, Radon (Rn), which has $Z = 86$.
After Radon, the $7\text{s}$, $5\text{f}$, $6\text{d}$, and $7\text{p}$ subshells are filled.
The total number of electrons is:
$Z = 86 \text{ (Rn)} + 2 \text{ (7s)} + 14 \text{ (5f)} + 10 \text{ (6d)} + 2 \text{ (7p)} = 114$.

For $Z = 114$, the IUPAC nomenclature uses the roots:
1 = un
1 = un
4 = quad

The name of the element is Ununquadium, and its three-letter IUPAC symbol is formed by taking the first letter of each root: Uuq.

Answer: Uuq

questions.q: The correct increasing order of the second ionization enthalpies of $\text{C}$, $\text{N}$, $\text{O}$ and $\text{F}$ is
questions.question: The correct increasing order of the second ionization enthalpies of $\text{C}$, $\text{N}$, $\text{O}$ and $\text{F}$ is
questions.solution:
The second ionization enthalpy is the energy required to remove an electron from the corresponding monopositive ion.

The electronic configurations of the $+1$ ions are:
$\text{C}^+ : [\text{He}] 2s^2 2p^1$
$\text{N}^+ : [\text{He}] 2s^2 2p^2$
$\text{O}^+ : [\text{He}] 2s^2 2p^3$
$\text{F}^+ : [\text{He}] 2s^2 2p^4$

Generally, ionization enthalpy increases from left to right as effective nuclear charge increases. However, $\text{O}^+$ has a highly stable half-filled $2p^3$ configuration. Due to this extra stability, the removal of an electron from $\text{O}^+$ requires more energy than from $\text{F}^+$.

Thus, the second ionization enthalpy of Oxygen is greater than that of Fluorine. The correct increasing order is $\text{C} < \text{N} < \text{F} < \text{O}$.

Answer: $\text{C} < \text{N} < \text{F} < \text{O}$

questions.question:
The first ionisation enthalpies (IE) and electron gain enthalpies (EGE) of four elements P, Q, R and S are given below in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$:

ElementIEEGE
P400-40
Q600-60

Which of the following pairs of elements will combine to form the compound with the highest ionic character?
questions.solution:
For a compound to have the highest ionic character, the electronegativity difference between the combining elements must be maximum.

This condition is met when one element easily forms a cation (has the lowest ionisation enthalpy) and the other easily forms an anion (has the most negative electron gain enthalpy).

From the given data, element P has the lowest ionisation enthalpy ($400 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) and element S has the most negative electron gain enthalpy ($-350 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$).

Therefore, the compound formed by P and S will have the highest ionic character.

Answer: PS

Graph A shows a strictly decreasing curve.
Graph B shows a strictly increasing curve.
Graph C shows a curve that increases from $\text{F}$ to $\text{Cl}$, then decreases for $\text{Br}$ and $\text{I}$.
Graph D shows a curve that decreases from $\text{F}$ to $\text{Cl}$, then increases for $\text{Br}$ and $\text{I}$.

Which graph correctly represents the variation of the magnitude of electron gain enthalpy for the group-17 elements?
questions.question:
Four different graphs are plotted for the variation of a periodic property (on the y-axis) against the first four halogens ($\text{F}$, $\text{Cl}$, $\text{Br}$, $\text{I}$) arranged in increasing order of atomic number (on the x-axis).

Graph A shows a strictly decreasing curve.
Graph B shows a strictly increasing curve.
Graph C shows a curve that increases from $\text{F}$ to $\text{Cl}$, then decreases for $\text{Br}$ and $\text{I}$.
Graph D shows a curve that decreases from $\text{F}$ to $\text{Cl}$, then increases for $\text{Br}$ and $\text{I}$.

Which graph correctly represents the variation of the magnitude of electron gain enthalpy for the group-17 elements?
questions.solution:
The magnitude of electron gain enthalpy generally decreases down a group as the atomic size increases.

However, due to the very small size of the $\text{F}$ atom, there are strong interelectronic repulsions in its relatively compact $2\text{p}$ subshell. As a result, the incoming electron experiences less attraction compared to the larger $\text{Cl}$ atom.

Therefore, the magnitude of electron gain enthalpy increases from $\text{F}$ to $\text{Cl}$, and then follows the regular trend of decreasing from $\text{Cl}$ to $\text{Br}$ to $\text{I}$.

The order of magnitude is: $\text{Cl} > \text{F} > \text{Br} > \text{I}$.

This variation is correctly represented by Graph C, which shows an initial increase followed by a decrease.

Answer: Graph C

questions.q: The correct increasing order of the first ionization enthalpies of $\text{Mg}$, $\text{Al}$, $\text{P}$ and $\text{S}$ is
questions.question: The correct increasing order of the first ionization enthalpies of $\text{Mg}$, $\text{Al}$, $\text{P}$ and $\text{S}$ is
questions.solution:
The general trend is an increase in first ionization enthalpy across a period from left to right. However, there are exceptions due to stable electronic configurations.

Magnesium ($\text{Mg}$) has a completely filled $3s$ subshell ($[\text{Ne}] 3s^2$), making its ionization enthalpy higher than that of Aluminium ($\text{Al}$, $[\text{Ne}] 3s^2 3p^1$).

Phosphorus ($\text{P}$) has a stable half-filled $3p$ subshell ($[\text{Ne}] 3s^2 3p^3$), making its ionization enthalpy higher than that of Sulphur ($\text{S}$, $[\text{Ne}] 3s^2 3p^4$).

Therefore, the correct increasing order is $\text{Al} < \text{Mg} < \text{S} < \text{P}$.

Answer: $\text{Al} < \text{Mg} < \text{S} < \text{P}$

Consider the following statements regarding Group 14 elements and their compounds:
(A) $\mathrm{SnO}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{PbO}_{2}$ are amphoteric oxides.
(B) $\mathrm{PbO}_{2}$ is a strong oxidizing agent because the $+4$ oxidation state of $\mathrm{Pb}$ is less stable than the $+2$ state.
(C) Silicon forms the complex $[\mathrm{SiF}_{6}]^{2-}$ whereas carbon cannot form $[\mathrm{CF}_{6}]^{2-}$.
(D) The acidic character of dioxides increases down the group.

Choose the correct combination of statements from the options given below.
questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding Group 14 elements and their compounds:
(A) $\mathrm{SnO}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{PbO}_{2}$ are amphoteric oxides.
(B) $\mathrm{PbO}_{2}$ is a strong oxidizing agent because the $+4$ oxidation state of $\mathrm{Pb}$ is less stable than the $+2$ state.
(C) Silicon forms the complex $[\mathrm{SiF}_{6}]^{2-}$ whereas carbon cannot form $[\mathrm{CF}_{6}]^{2-}$.
(D) The acidic character of dioxides increases down the group.

Choose the correct combination of statements from the options given below.
questions.solution:
Statement (A) is correct. The dioxides of carbon and silicon ($\mathrm{CO}_{2}$, $\mathrm{SiO}_{2}$) are acidic, $\mathrm{GeO}_{2}$ is distinctly acidic but weakly amphoteric, while $\mathrm{SnO}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{PbO}_{2}$ are amphoteric in nature.

Statement (B) is correct. Due to the inert pair effect, the $+2$ oxidation state is more stable than the $+4$ state for lead. Thus, $\mathrm{PbO}_{2}$ readily gets reduced to $\mathrm{Pb}^{2+}$, acting as a strong oxidizing agent.

Statement (C) is correct. Silicon has vacant d-orbitals in its valence shell, allowing it to expand its coordination number to 6 and form $[\mathrm{SiF}_{6}]^{2-}$. Carbon lacks d-orbitals and is restricted to a maximum covalency of 4, so it cannot form $[\mathrm{CF}_{6}]^{2-}$.

Statement (D) is incorrect. The acidic character of dioxides decreases down the group as the metallic character of the elements increases.

Therefore, the correct statements are (A), (B), and (C).

Answer: (A), (B) and (C) only

questions.q:
Four consecutive p-block elements in the second period of the periodic table have atomic numbers $Z$, $Z+1$, $Z+2$, and $Z+3$. Their first ionization enthalpies ($\Delta_{i}H_{1}$) are observed to follow the order:

$\Delta_{i}H_{1}(Z) < \Delta_{i}H_{1}(Z+2) < \Delta_{i}H_{1}(Z+1) < \Delta_{i}H_{1}(Z+3)$

The outermost electronic configuration of the element with atomic number $Z+2$ is:
questions.question:
Four consecutive p-block elements in the second period of the periodic table have atomic numbers $Z$, $Z+1$, $Z+2$, and $Z+3$. Their first ionization enthalpies ($\Delta_{i}H_{1}$) are observed to follow the order:

$\Delta_{i}H_{1}(Z) < \Delta_{i}H_{1}(Z+2) < \Delta_{i}H_{1}(Z+1) < \Delta_{i}H_{1}(Z+3)$

The outermost electronic configuration of the element with atomic number $Z+2$ is:
questions.solution:
For consecutive p-block elements in the second period, the first ionization enthalpy generally increases with atomic number due to increasing effective nuclear charge.

However, an exception occurs between Group 15 and Group 16. Group 15 elements have a stable half-filled p-orbital configuration ($\mathrm{ns}^{2} \mathrm{np}^{3}$), which requires more energy to remove an electron compared to the $\mathrm{ns}^{2} \mathrm{np}^{4}$ configuration of Group 16 elements.

The given order shows a dip where the element with atomic number $Z+2$ has a lower ionization enthalpy than the element with atomic number $Z+1$. This indicates that $Z+1$ is a Group 15 element (Nitrogen) and $Z+2$ is a Group 16 element (Oxygen).

The sequence of elements is Carbon ($Z$), Nitrogen ($Z+1$), Oxygen ($Z+2$), and Fluorine ($Z+3$).

The element with atomic number $Z+2$ is Oxygen, and its outermost electronic configuration is $2\mathrm{s}^{2} 2\mathrm{p}^{4}$.

Answer: $2\mathrm{s}^{2} 2\mathrm{p}^{4}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Identify the incorrect statement among the following.
questions.question: Identify the incorrect statement among the following.
options: The third ionization enthalpy of $\text{Al}$ is significantly greater than the third ionization enthalpy of $\text{Mg}$.
The second ionization enthalpy of $\text{Cu}$ is higher than the second ionization enthalpy of $\text{Zn}$.
The second ionization enthalpy of $\text{Cr}$ is higher than the second ionization enthalpy of $\text{Mn}$.
The first ionization enthalpy of $\text{Zn}$ is higher than the first ionization enthalpy of $\text{Ga}$.
questions.solution:
Let us evaluate each statement by writing the electronic configurations of the relevant atoms and ions.

For $\text{Mg}$ ($Z=12$): The configuration is $[\text{Ne}] 3s^2$. After removing two electrons, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ attains the stable noble gas configuration of Neon ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$). Removing a third electron requires breaking this highly stable core, so the third ionization enthalpy ($IE_3$) of $\text{Mg}$ is extremely high.
For $\text{Al}$ ($Z=13$): The configuration is $[\text{Ne}] 3s^2 3p^1$. After removing two electrons, $\text{Al}^{2+}$ has the configuration $[\text{Ne}] 3s^1$. Removing the third electron is relatively easy as it removes the last valence electron. Thus, $IE_3$ of $\text{Mg} > IE_3$ of $\text{Al}$. The statement claiming $IE_3$ of $\text{Al} > IE_3$ of $\text{Mg}$ is incorrect.

For $\text{Cu}$ ($Z=29$) and $\text{Zn}$ ($Z=30$): $\text{Cu}^+$ is $[\text{Ar}] 3d^{10}$ and $\text{Zn}^+$ is $[\text{Ar}] 3d^{10} 4s^1$. The second ionization of $\text{Cu}$ disrupts a fully filled $3d^{10}$ subshell, whereas for $\text{Zn}$ it removes a $4s$ electron. Hence, $IE_2$ of $\text{Cu} > IE_2$ of $\text{Zn}$.

For $\text{Cr}$ ($Z=24$) and $\text{Mn}$ ($Z=25$): $\text{Cr}^+$ is $[\text{Ar}] 3d^5$ and $\text{Mn}^+$ is $[\text{Ar}] 3d^5 4s^1$. The second ionization of $\text{Cr}$ disrupts a stable half-filled $3d^5$ subshell, whereas for $\text{Mn}$ it removes a $4s$ electron. Hence, $IE_2$ of $\text{Cr} > IE_2$ of $\text{Mn}$.

For $\text{Zn}$ ($Z=30$) and $\text{Ga}$ ($Z=31$): $\text{Zn}$ has a fully filled configuration $[\text{Ar}] 3d^{10} 4s^2$, while $\text{Ga}$ is $[\text{Ar}] 3d^{10} 4s^2 4p^1$. Removing the $4p$ electron from $\text{Ga}$ requires less energy than breaking the fully filled $4s$ subshell of $\text{Zn}$. Hence, $IE_1$ of $\text{Zn} > IE_1$ of $\text{Ga}$.

Answer: The third ionization enthalpy of $\text{Al}$ is significantly greater than the third ionization enthalpy of $\text{Mg}$.

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The first ionization enthalpy of Gallium is marginally higher than that of Aluminum.
Reason (R): The presence of $10$ d-electrons in Gallium offers poor shielding effect for the valence electrons.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The first ionization enthalpy of Gallium is marginally higher than that of Aluminum.
Reason (R): The presence of $10$ d-electrons in Gallium offers poor shielding effect for the valence electrons.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Normally, ionization enthalpy decreases down a group. However, Gallium follows immediately after the $3\text{d}$ transition series.

The $10$ d-electrons in Ga provide poor shielding against the increased nuclear charge, leading to a higher effective nuclear charge on the valence electrons. This makes the ionization enthalpy of Ga slightly higher than Al.

Thus, both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation.

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In Group 16, oxygen has the least negative electron gain enthalpy among all the elements in the group.

Statement II: In Group 17, fluorine has the least negative electron gain enthalpy among all the elements in the group.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In Group 16, oxygen has the least negative electron gain enthalpy among all the elements in the group.

Statement II: In Group 17, fluorine has the least negative electron gain enthalpy among all the elements in the group.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.solution:
Statement I is correct. In Group 16, the electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is the least negative ($\approx -141 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) compared to the rest of the group members (e.g., S is $\approx -200 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, Po is $\approx -174 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$). This is due to the very small size of the oxygen atom, which leads to strong interelectronic repulsions when an extra electron is added.

Statement II is incorrect. In Group 17, although fluorine has a less negative electron gain enthalpy ($\approx -328 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) than chlorine ($\approx -349 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) due to similar interelectronic repulsions, it is still more negative than those of bromine ($\approx -325 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) and iodine ($\approx -295 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$). Thus, fluorine does not have the least negative electron gain enthalpy in Group 17.

Therefore, Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

This leads to a significant increase in the effective nuclear charge (lanthanide contraction effect), making the first ionization enthalpy of Tl higher than that of Al. The overall order of first ionization enthalpy for Group 13 is B > Tl > Ga > Al > In.

Statement II is correct: Gallium (Period 4) contains 3d electrons that offer poor shielding (scandide contraction). This causes its valence electrons to be pulled closer to the nucleus, making its atomic radius (135 pm) smaller than that of Aluminum (143 pm).

Therefore, both statements are correct.

The IUPAC name 'Unnilseptium' can be decoded using the numerical roots for elements with $Z > 100$:
un = 1
nil = 0
sept = 7
Thus, the atomic number of the element is $Z = 107$.

The nearest preceding noble gas is Radon (Rn), which has an atomic number of $86$.
The number of electrons to be filled after Radon is $107 - 86 = 21$.

According to the Aufbau principle, these $21$ electrons are distributed into the $7\text{s}$, $5\text{f}$, and $6\text{d}$ subshells.
Filling order: $7\text{s}$ takes $2$ electrons, $5\text{f}$ takes $14$ electrons, and the remaining $5$ electrons enter the $6\text{d}$ subshell.

Therefore, the outer electronic configuration is $[\text{Rn}] 5\text{f}^{14} 6\text{d}^{5} 7\text{s}^{2}$.

Answer: $[\text{Rn}] 5\text{f}^{14} 6\text{d}^{5} 7\text{s}^{2}$
